sections.question: What policy changes, government announcements and implementation evidence concern climate and energy across the public record since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Across the Australian public record since July 2024, climate and energy policy activity spans federal and Victorian jurisdictions. In federal parliament, a senator moved to refer to the Environment and Communications References Committee "the Government's secrecy and withholding of the Climate Risk Assessment (the assessment) from the Australian public since December 2024," with a report due by 20 November 2025. A government response to a Portfolio Committee report on "Planning system and the impacts of climate change on the environment and communities" was published on 17 February 2025, and a response to the Net Zero Commission's annual report for the year ended 30 June 2024 was received on 26 February 2025 under the Climate Change (Net Zero Future) Act 2023. A private senator's bill, the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Climate Trigger) Bill 2022, was also moved for consideration in July 2025.

On implementation evidence, a federal senator claimed that "more home batteries were installed in the first six weeks of this program than in the first six months of 2024" and that "we hit 40,000 batteries since July," describing this as "public policy that is working." The same speaker cited Australian Conservation Foundation reporting that by 2030 "the increased level of solar and batteries will lift renewable energy's share of the power supply by 4.5 per cent above that estimated in AEMO's current projections." A motion was also moved to table documents from the Clean Energy Regulator concerning the Cheaper Home Batteries Program for July–August 2025 and February 2026. In estimates, a departmental official said a government procurement policy was "already seeing results" at the Commonwealth level, and another official corrected a figure, noting a December quarter 2024 CPI release "reported a 25.2 per cent decline in electricity prices over the previous 12 months," not a comparison back to 2022.

On targets and funding, a federal senator stated the government had "committed over $70 billion to action on climate change" since 2022, citing Budget Paper No. 1, and referenced a "$5 billion Net Zero Fund under the National Reconstruction Fund" among announced measures. The same speaker said the government's 62 to 70 per cent target was supported by the safeguard mechanism, the national vehicle emissions scheme and other measures. A departmental official confirmed the first instrument under new legislation "was given life to in December 2024, so that's 12 months after the legislation." In Victoria, a state MP spoke on the Strategic Audit 2022–23, noting the report found departments must make "considerable progress to reduce net GHG emissions from their operations" to meet the state's net zero and interim targets, and claimed Victoria's emissions "have declined by 27.6 per cent between 1990 and 2021" while the economy grew 126 per cent, with per capita emissions "well below the national average." The MP also said the government remains committed to "net zero by 2045."

sections.question: What do bills, government releases, contracts, grants and disclosure records reveal about climate and energy, and what remains unproven since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Bills, government releases, grants and disclosure records since July 2024 show a mix of delivered measures, announced targets and contested transparency. On climate and energy delivery, the Prime Minister and the Minister for Climate Change and Energy stated that "507,651 home batteries installed since the 1st of July last year" — described as "Half a million, which is a remarkable national achievement" — and that "125,000 households since July 1, have taken up the opportunity of the support from the Federal Government to install batteries." Minister Chris Bowen added that this represents "14 gigawatt hours' worth of storage. That compares to 9 gigawatt hours in all of the United States." The Prime Minister also claimed the government has "one policy. We're delivering it. The Net Zero by 2050, 43 per cent reduction by 2030, the rollout of renewables backed by gas, backed by batteries, the Safeguard Mechanism... as well as the Capacity Investment Scheme." These are ministerial claims of delivery, not independent verification.

NSW government releases describe phased climate disclosure obligations: "NSW climate disclosures are being phased in over three years, starting with the most climate exposed departments, agencies and state-owned corporations," with "An initial 29 government entities" publishing disclosures in 2024-25 annual reports and "An additional 30 entities" from 2025-26, ahead of "a first whole-of-government climate-related financial disclosure next year." NSW also reported that "More than $180 million in benefits have been committed to communities since the guideline's introduction in November 2024," and that "The Minns Labor Government invested $3.5 billion in Climate Change and Energy initiatives in the 2024-25 Budget, including $3.1 billion in NSW's Renewable Energy Zones." A NSW release also states "The NSW Government secured an agreement with Origin Energy in 2024 to underwrite Eraring until August 2027, to ensure energy reliability and avoid price spikes." Separately, NSW Minister for Climate Change and Energy Penny Sharpe is quoted: "Households are looking for practical ways to bring down their energy bills, and this funding will help put trusted advice and support within easier reach." These are state government announcements of commitments and funding, not proof of expenditure or outcomes.

On transparency, Senate divisions show repeated opposition attempts to force production of documents from the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW) and the Clean Energy Finance Corporation. On 26 August 2025 the Senate referred to the Environment and Communications References Committee an inquiry into "the Government's secrecy and withholding of the Climate Risk Assessment (the assessment) from the Australian public since December 2024" — carried 34–25. On 20 November 2024 the Senate ordered production of documents concerning DCCEEW's FOI review LEX 77481 relating to Coomera Connector stage 1, noting appendices on koala research, koala translocation and Coastal Swamp Oak TEC were "entirely redacted" — carried 39–15. On 9 October 2024 a similar order was defeated 29–29, with the Senate noting the Minister had provided "a link to a document" that "was not the document being sought." On 30 June 2026 the Senate ordered production of Clean Energy Finance Corporation documents on any financial support considered or provided — carried 34–20. On 25 June 2026 a motion to produce Climate Change and Energy portfolio Senate estimates briefs was defeated 24–32, and on 3 March 2026 a motion to produce DCCEEW "hot issues/Senate estimates briefs" was defeated 24–39. These divisions record parliamentary votes, not findings of wrongdoing.

What remains unproven includes the actual content of the Climate Risk Assessment, which the Senate motion asserts was withheld "from the Australian public since December 2024" — the motion itself is a parliamentary reference, not evidence of what the assessment contains. Similarly, the Senate motions reference non-compliance with orders for documents, but no passage establishes what those documents would show. The Treasury Laws Amendment (Financial Market Infrastructure and Other Measures) Bill 2024 saw opposition amendments on "scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions and removing group 3 entities" defeated 26–35 in committee on 22 August 2024; the passage records the vote but not the substance of the debate. A report on dwelling prices notes "The supply forecasts do not directly incorporate the impacts of recent state government policy measures related to land use reform," which is a limitation of forecasting, not a climate or energy finding. No passage provides independent verification of the claimed battery numbers, emissions reductions, or the $180 million in community benefits — those figures rest on government statements.

sections.answer:

A Greens-aligned speaker reflected on supporting "the government to legislate a 43 per cent emissions reduction target by 2030" in the 47th Parliament and urged support for the Climate Change (National Framework for Adaptation) Bill 2025. sections.question: What has been said in parliament about coal mining and the transition to renewable energy since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Coal mining and the energy transition have been debated extensively in New South Wales and federal parliaments since July 2024. In the NSW Legislative Assembly, a Labor member supporting the Energy Legislation Amendment (Prioritising Renewable Energy) Bill 2026 said the state's plan has "historically been underpinned by multipartisan support," with three of four coal-fired power stations scheduled to retire by 2033 and the last by 2040, meaning "thermal coal in New South Wales is being replaced." A Greens member warned that coalmining is "responsible for about 12 per cent of the State's emissions" and that recent approvals for expansions at Moolarben, Boggabri, Glendell, Narrabri, Ravensworth, Mount Pleasant, Ulan and Tahmoor, plus 17 applications in the pipeline, mean New South Wales "will not achieve its targets." The member called for the Net Zero Commission to assess every coal application and for the "outdated and discredited Strategic Statement on Coal Exploration and Mining in NSW" to be revoked.

In the NSW Legislative Council, Minister Penny Sharpe said the renewable energy roadmap "is well underway and is being delivered," citing HumeLink, the South West and Central-West Orana renewable energy zones, and new solar and batteries, while noting "our old coal‑fired power stations continued to struggle" with 90 unscheduled outages in the 2025-26 summer. She said taxpayers have "not paid not one cent to extend Eraring." In response to a question about Peabody's Wilpinjong Mine application near Wollar, Minister Courtney Houssos said it "will be assessed in accordance with our robust assessment process" and pointed to the Future Jobs and Investment Bill 2025 to plan for the roughly 25,000 direct coalmining jobs.

Federal debate also covered the issue. In the Senate, a motion on climate change and three new coal mines was defeated 12–26 on 8 October 2024. A Coalition senator argued the Labor government's transition "has not been technology-agnostic" and "has been unreasonable," with regional communities "largely had to pay the price." A Labor senator responded that the government has approved "some 130 new renewable energy projects since being elected in 2022." In the House of Representatives, a Labor speaker said that under the previous Coalition government, "24 out of Australia's 28 coal-fired power stations announced their closure" with "no replacement plan," whereas renewables supplied half of the national electricity market last month. Labor MPs also spoke in support of the Coal Mining Industry (Long Service Leave) Legislation Amendment Bill 2025, with the member for Hunter describing his years as a coalminer and the bill's importance to "fairness, certainty and respect."

sections.question: How have MPs discussed carbon pricing and its repeal since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Carbon pricing has been discussed in several parliamentary estimates hearings since July 2024, with the most detailed exchanges occurring in the Environment and Communications Legislation Committee on 7 October 2025. In that hearing, a senator characterised the government's carbon abatement modelling as looking "and smells very much like a price on carbon: a carbon tax," asking whether an official would agree with that characterisation. Another participant in the same hearing described the modelled incentive as "an economy-wide marginal abatement incentive which, by 2050, will reach up to $328 based on 2024 dollars," contrasting this with the Gillard government's carbon price of "between $20 and $40" and calling the Treasury figure of "$293 and $328" an "alarming increase for every single tonne of abatement."

In the Rural and Regional Affairs and Transport Legislation Committee on 2 December 2025, a senator pursued the same modelling, noting that Treasury had projected a carbon price "in the 2046 to 2050 period of between $293 a tonne and $328 a tonne" and asking whether the department's estimates of the relationship between carbon price and sequestration were "in that order." Separately, in the Infrastructure Australia estimates on 9 February 2026, an official explained that carbon values have been applied to business cases since February 2024, with the impact found to be "relatively marginal," and that the work standardises "in alignment with federal law what the least cost would be to achieve the targets set at federal law."

The record also contains references to carbon market administration rather than pricing levels. In a Finance and Public Administration hearing on 1 December 2025, a speaker mentioned a "comprehensive package of reforms to strengthen integrity, improve transparency, increase fairness and streamline administration" for the carbon market, noting consultations occurred "in 2023, and on this bill in 2026." No passage in the retrieved record discusses the repeal of carbon pricing, and the record is limited to these estimates committee exchanges and related portfolio statements.

sections.question: What has parliament said about Energy policy?
sections.answer:
Parliamentary debate on energy policy is sharply partisan, with each side blaming the other for failures. Coalition speakers claimed the Albanese Labor government's policy is "based on ideology, not reality," citing the unfulfilled election promise of a "$275 cut to power bills" while "most Australians have seen their power bills increase by a thousand dollars." One Coalition member said the government has "completely and utterly stuffed energy policy," and another asserted the opposition's "No. 1 priority will be to reduce electricity prices." A government senator responded that the Coalition "had almost 10 years to put an energy policy in place, and they failed," noting that during their time in government "24 out of 28 coal-fired power stations announced they were closing" and that they had "23 different policies which came and went."

In the New South Wales parliament, a Labor member highlighted that the Climate Change (Net Zero Future) Act 2023, setting targets of "a 50 per cent reduction on 2005 emissions by 2030, a 70 per cent reduction on 2005 emissions by 2035 and net zero emissions by 2050," had "bipartisan support" from Labor and the Liberal-Nationals Coalition. However, the same member expressed fear that "members opposite are seeking to undermine that commitment," pointing to Nationals MPs who said "We are not opposed, but" and to the Commonwealth Nationals "undermining our national commitment to net zero." A NSW Liberal member countered that "energy bills on average have risen by 20 per cent under the Minns Labor Government, despite wholesale prices dropping," and cited the independent Net Zero Commission stating "there is no chance we will meet the Government's own legislated net zero targets."

At estimates hearings, a Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water official said the government "has legislated its commitment to 43 per cent reductions by 2030" and "continues to track its progress towards that target." A government senator described energy security as "industrial policy; it is economic policy," and criticised One Nation and "some of their friends in the Nationals and the Liberals" for "retweeting propaganda." Another government senator accused the Coalition of having "22 energy policies and didn't land one of them" in government, plus a nuclear policy in opposition, making "23 energy policies they haven't been able to land."

sections.question: What has parliament said about Waste and recycling management and climate and energy?
sections.answer:
Parliamentary records show ongoing scrutiny of waste and recycling policy, particularly around the delayed review of the Recycling and Waste Reduction Act 2020. In a 2026 estimates hearing, a senator challenged the department: "There's been no legislation before parliament under this government in the waste space—nearly four years. Why don't we actually just do something?" Departmental official Mr Tregurtha responded that the review had been extended in 2025 to consider issues like plastic waste exports, and that the department was "finalising the RAWR Act review and providing advice on options to government," including on extended producer responsibility. He noted the review report was expected to be delivered to the minister "imminently" and would be tabled in parliament.

Senate inquiry reports on waste have drawn criticism. One committee record states that recommendations "supported by the community, environmental advocates and waste management and recycling peak bodies... have consistently been ignored by consecutive governments, resulting in our current state of affairs, which sees waste increasing, more packaging being sent to landfill and recycling rates remaining stagnant." On government procurement of recycled products, a senator noted industry feedback that "governments aren't procuring anything from the sector," questioning how that reconciles with the need for markets for recycled product.

On climate and energy, a department official stated that "the government has legislated its commitment to 43 per cent reductions by 2030" and "continues to track its progress towards that target, including through statements to parliament each year by the climate change minister." In a separate exchange, a minister defended the government's approach as "a practical, commonsense plan to achieve objectives like getting the electricity system to 82 per cent and to make sure that electricity for households is the lowest cost, most reliable framework; renewables and storage backed up by gas-peaking capability."

On waste-to-energy, a minister said any proposal "needs to go through proper processes in local communities and planning processes," adding that "there is a role for waste to energy in our circular economy" and that communities "are entitled to utilise those processes." NSW Minister Penny Sharpe, in a state parliamentary context, said of energy-from-waste: "landfill is the worst solution for getting rid of waste. Energy from waste is the slightly less bad way of dealing with those things," while acknowledging communities "are right to ask the questions."

sections.question: What has parliament said about Timber Industry and Great Koala National Park and climate and energy?
sections.answer:
The New South Wales Parliament has extensively debated the Great Koala National Park and its impact on the timber industry. The Hon. Tania Mihailuk moved a motion noting that a "Timber Talks" event was hosted at NSW Parliament House on 13 February 2025, and citing a 2023 Ernst & Young study estimating the NSW hardwood industry generated approximately $2.9 billion in annual revenue and supported around 8,900 full-time equivalent jobs in 2021-22. The motion also noted the Government's commitment of $80 million over four years to develop the park, and called on the Government to consult with timber industry workers. The Hon. Penny Sharpe, Minister for Climate Change, Energy, Environment and Heritage, responded that the Government had placed a moratorium on harvesting within the proposed 176,000-hectare park boundary, and that the park would require legislation to be passed by Parliament.

Opposition and crossbench members criticised the Government's handling of the transition. The Hon. Sarah Mitchell, leader of the Nationals, said the decision "will obliterate the North Coast timber industry," and quoted a text from a timber industry family: "How do I tell my two grandchildren today, on Father's Day, that Poppy will have to sack their dad and both their uncles?" The Hon. Mark Banasiak of the Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party accused the Government of treating forestry workers as "collateral damage in a political playpen." In contrast, Ms Sue Higginson of The Greens said the industry "has come to the end of its life," citing Forestry Corporation's annual report showing the hardwood industry lost $29 million last year. Minister Sharpe stated that over 90 per cent of timber required for housing is softwood, not hardwood, and that the Government is committed to a "Forestry Industry Action Plan" for the future.

On climate and energy, the record is more limited. Minister Sharpe noted the Government has "put forward for assessment a forest method that, if adopted, would provide an opportunity for there to be carbon credits within the area of the park," with that independent process being assessed by the Federal Government. The Hon. Gurmesh Singh of The Nationals alleged the park "has nothing to do with protecting habitats. It is about protecting the Treasurer so that he can sell the carbon credits generated by the park." Minister Sharpe also cited economic analysis calculating "$163 million and around 85,000 extra nights in the Mid North Coast region from tourism" as a result of the park.

eras.label: 1993–2009
eras.question: How did policy and public debate develop on climate and energy between 1993 and 2009? The debates of the period included Climate Change, Tax Laws Amendment (2008 Measures No. 1) Bill 2008 and Water Amendment Bill 2008.
eras.answer:
Climate and energy policy developed through a series of legislative debates in the Australian Parliament between 2008 and 2009, framed by the Rudd Labor government’s claims of action after "more than a decade of lost opportunities under the Howard government." In one speech, the government said it had "ratified the Kyoto protocol, designed and introduced legislation on the Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme, decided on a renewable energy target, invested $4.5 billion in clean energy initiatives, developed the Solar Flagships program, implemented the Solar Homes and Communities Plan, invested $4 billion in the Energy Efficient Homes package and committed $12.9 billion towards a national water strategy." A senator supporting the Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2009 called the package "some of the most important pieces of legislation that the Rudd government will be dealing with" for their "potential economic and environmental impact."

Public debate included criticism and alternative proposals. One speaker said the Appropriation Bills for 2008-2009 "do not adequately reflect the urgency of climate change," and described a petition with over 1,000 signatures calling for steps such as signing the Kyoto protocol, setting mandatory emissions targets, halting public funding for fossil fuel industries, phasing out coal-fired power stations, and investing in public transport. Another speaker, referring to the earlier Howard government’s Mandatory Renewable Energy Target, said the Labor opposition’s 2007 election promise to lift it "from its pitifully and unpopularly low 2 per cent up to 20 per cent" was welcomed by the Greens and environment groups "as a significant improvement, although not as much as is both achievable and necessary." A senator also expressed "significant reservations about the model proposed by Professor Garnaut" for an emissions trading scheme, while noting the minister was reported as "looking at other emissions trading models."

The record also links climate debate to other bills. One speaker supported the Water Amendment Bill 2008 "generally" but noted "significant room for improvement with amendments," and another criticised the Howard government’s record on climate change in the same debate. The Tax Laws Amendment (2008 Measures No. 1) Bill 2008 was debated partly in connection with electoral matters, with one senator complaining that the chamber was "not actually debating the amendments but debating a whole range of different issues around climate change." The passages do not provide detail on policy development before 2008, and the record retrieved is limited to these 2008-2009 parliamentary exchanges.

eras.label: 2010–2019
eras.question: How did policy and public debate develop on climate and energy between 2010 and 2019? The debates of the period included Biodiversity Conservation Bill 2016; Local Land Services Amendment Bill 2016, Water Management Amendment Bill 2018 and Water Supply (Critical Needs) Bill 2019.
eras.answer:
In November 2016, New South Wales enacted the Biodiversity Conservation Act and the Local Land Services Amendment Act, which were described as integrating and modernising laws governing biodiversity conservation and threatened species management. The then Minister for Resources, Energy and Utilities, and the Arts, Don Harwin, stated the reforms included an "unprecedented investment of $240 million over five years and $70 million in each following year for a new private land conservation program." A petition received from Justin Field called on the government to repeal both the Local Land Services Amendment Act 2016 and the Biodiversity Conservation Act 2016, and to enact laws protecting the environment and wildlife and preserving native vegetation as carbon sinks. The government also advised it would publish submissions and a submissions report online when those bills were introduced into Parliament.

On climate and energy policy more broadly, the record includes debate on the Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2010 and related bills, which were said to implement an enhanced renewable energy target, separating the scheme into the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme and the large-scale renewable energy target from 1 January 2011. A senator supporting the Clean Energy Amendment (International Emissions Trading and Other Measures) Bill 2012 noted the government had first announced changes to the scheme in November 2010, with the changes subject to consideration and examination, including by a Senate committee that reported in May. An opposition senator characterised the government as "in chaos" over its climate policy, changing it "just after a few months" and doing the opposite of what was promised. A separate amendment to the Water Act was described as ensuring any Basin Plan must continuously take into account the most up-to-date science on climate change, with the Guide to the Basin Plan released in 2010 proposing a reallocation of diverted water to the environment over 10 years for adaptation.

On the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment Bill 2013, which sought to add a new matter of national environmental significance for coal seam gas or large coalmining developments with significant impacts on a water resource, a House committee declined to conduct its own inquiry, noting the bill had been referred to the Senate Environment and Communications Legislation Committee, which had suggested six specific and two general sources of evidence and five possible hearing dates. A senator contributing to debate on that bill noted the Senate committee received 235 submissions from industry, environmental groups and the community. The record also lists the Water Supply (Critical Needs) Bill 2019 among bills not referred to a standing committee for inquiry, as moved by Natasha Maclaren-Jones in the New South Wales Legislative Council on 22 October 2019.

eras.label: 2020–2024
eras.question: How did policy and public debate develop on climate and energy between 2020 and the middle of 2024? The debates of the period included Electricity Infrastructure Investment Bill 2020, Bushfires and Energy policy.
eras.answer:
The New South Wales Parliament debated and passed the Electricity Infrastructure Investment Bill 2020, with speakers describing it as a shift away from coal and toward renewables. One Labor member said the bill was "a win for evidence and science" and "a win for renewables," and that it promised savings of "$130 a year" for households and "$440 a year" for small businesses, while noting the plan was imperfect. The Animal Justice Party's Emma Hurst expressed support, saying the bill "signals a much-needed shift in government policy and investment away from outdated coal-fired power and towards clean renewable energy," and that it could increase New South Wales renewables from about 16 per cent to more than 60 per cent by 2030. A later ministerial reply confirmed that section 23 of the Electricity Infrastructure Investment Act 2020 legislates that the minister will declare the Illawarra and Hunter‑Central Coast Renewable Energy Zones.

Public debate in the period also linked climate change to bushfire risk. In August 2020, Rose Jackson noted the NSW Bushfire Inquiry found "climate change played a role" in the 2019-20 fire season and that New South Wales should expect similar or worse seasons, criticising the Cabinet for instead debating uranium mining. A Victorian MP, speaking on the National Energy Legislation Amendment Bill 2020, called 2020 a "dumpster fire of a year" marked by bushfire smoke and COVID, and urged governments to invest in a "Green New Deal" with publicly owned renewables, storage, energy efficiency retrofits and nature restoration. Federal speakers in 2024 criticised the Coalition for "climate denial" and for calling net zero targets "ideological," while a government senator said the previous government's "lack of a settled climate policy" and "22 policies. None of them landed in a decade" had caused problems in the energy sector. Another federal speaker noted that in 2022 the government legislated "a 43 per cent emissions reduction by 2030 and net zero by 2050" and committed "$20 billion" to upgrade the energy grid.

lede.text: Australia’s climate and energy argument is fundamentally about whether legislated net zero should be delivered through renewables and storage backed by gas, with energy security, reliability and household cost as the governing tests. Labor presents its 43 per cent 2030 target, 82 per cent renewable electricity objective and new generation as a practical economic transition, while Coalition speakers attack unmet $275 bill savings and rising prices. The immediate contest concerns how far ambition and scrutiny should go, from the proposed 62 to 70 per cent 2035 target and stronger Greens demands to Senate battles over the withheld Climate Risk Assessment. Over time, debate has moved from the 2008, 09 Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme and renewable energy targets, through 2020 legislation replacing ageing coal, toward implementation, transparency and the pace of coal’s retirement.
